Eugenics is the belief — and the set of practices based on that belief — that the human species can be deliberately improved by controlling who is allowed (or encouraged) to reproduce, and who is not.

Think of it like this: farmers have been selectively breeding animals for thousands of years. They breed the strongest horses with other strong horses to get even stronger offspring. They breed cows that produce the most milk, dogs with the calmest temperaments, and so on. Eugenics is the idea of applying that same logic to human beings — deciding which people should have children and which should not, based on their traits.

People who have promoted eugenics throughout history wanted to increase traits they considered desirable, such as:

  • High intelligence
  • Physical health and strength
  • Freedom from hereditary diseases

And they wanted to reduce traits they considered undesirable, such as:

  • Mental illness
  • Physical disabilities
  • Low intelligence (as they defined and measured it)

Here is where the first major problem begins: deciding which traits are "desirable" or "undesirable" is not a scientific question — it is a values question. And historically, those in power answered it in deeply biased, racist, and classist ways. "Desirable" almost always meant traits common in the white, wealthy, educated class. "Undesirable" almost always meant traits associated with poor people, ethnic minorities, immigrants, or the disabled.

Eugenics has generally been practiced in two ways:

1. Positive Eugenics
This encourages people with "desirable" traits to have more children. Examples include financial incentives for certain people to have large families, or propaganda campaigns urging "fit" people to marry each other and reproduce.

2. Negative Eugenics
This discourages or outright prevents people with "undesirable" traits from having children. This is far more sinister and has included:

  • Forced sterilization (surgically removing a person's ability to have children without their consent)
  • Marriage laws that banned certain people from marrying
  • Immigration restrictions to keep out people from certain ethnic backgrounds
  • In its most extreme form — mass murder, as carried out by the Nazis
The Historical Reality: A Dark Record

Eugenics is not just a theoretical idea. It was put into large-scale practice throughout the 20th century, with catastrophic results.

In the United States, eugenics became law. Over 60,000 Americans — including people with mental illness, epilepsy, low IQ scores, and even simply people who were poor or "promiscuous" — were forcibly sterilized, mostly between the 1920s and 1970s. The Supreme Court actually upheld this practice in 1927 (Buck v. Bell), a decision that has never been formally overturned.

In Nazi Germany, eugenics was taken to its most monstrous extreme. The Nazi regime sterilized around 400,000 people and ultimately used eugenic ideology as one of the justifications for the Holocaust — the systematic murder of six million Jewish people, along with hundreds of thousands of Roma, disabled people, gay people, and others deemed "unfit" by the state.

Eugenics programs also existed in Canada, Sweden, Australia, Japan, and many other countries.

Beyond the ethical horror, eugenics rests on bad science. Here is why:

Genetics is extraordinarily complex. Most human traits — intelligence, personality, health — are influenced by thousands of genes interacting with each other in ways we still don't fully understand. You cannot simply "breed out" a condition like mental illness the way you might breed a specific coat color into a dog.

Environment matters enormously. Intelligence, behavior, and health are heavily shaped by nutrition, education, poverty, stress, trauma, and social conditions — not just genes. A child born to intelligent parents but raised in poverty and deprivation may not flourish. A child born with "ordinary" genetics but raised in a rich, stimulating environment often does.

Genetic diversity is a strength. Many genes that cause disease in one context provide advantages in another. The gene variant that causes sickle cell disease, for example, also provides protection against malaria in one copy. Removing "bad" genes from the population would often remove beneficial ones at the same time.

The "undesirable traits" claim was often just prejudice. Many of the people sterilized or targeted were not actually carrying heritable conditions at all — they were simply poor, non-white, non-English-speaking, or mentally ill due to trauma and circumstances, none of which is straightforwardly "passed on" through genes.

Even if eugenics could work scientifically (and it largely cannot), it would still be profoundly wrong. Here is why:

It violates human dignity. Every person has inherent worth regardless of their genes, health, intelligence, or productivity. Deciding who is "fit" to reproduce treats human beings as livestock — as means to an end — rather than as individuals with rights.

It strips away bodily autonomy. The right to have children (or not) is one of the most personal decisions a human being can make. Forcibly taking that right away is one of the gravest violations of a person's freedom.

Power always corrupts the definition of "fit." Whoever holds power gets to decide what is desirable. In practice, this has always meant that the powerful — the wealthy, the ruling class, the dominant race — defined themselves as fit and everyone else as unfit. This is not science. It is oppression dressed up in scientific language.

The word "eugenics" is now almost universally recognized as a term for one of history's great moral failures. No mainstream government or scientific institution endorses it. It is considered a cautionary tale about what happens when pseudoscience and prejudice are weaponized by state power.

However, the concept continues to surface in new and debated forms:

Genetic screening allows parents to test embryos for severe genetic diseases before implantation during IVF. Most ethicists consider this acceptable when it is a voluntary choice by parents to avoid serious suffering — because it does not involve force or state control.

Gene editing technologies like CRISPR raise new questions about whether editing human embryos to remove disease genes is ethically permissible, or whether it slides into eugenic territory.

The line most ethicists draw is this: individual, voluntary choice to avoid severe disease for your own child is not eugenics. State-enforced or socially coerced control over who reproduces, or selection based on social prejudices about "superior" traits, is.

Eugenics is the idea and practice of trying to "improve" the human species by controlling human reproduction — promoting reproduction among people seen as having desirable traits, and preventing it among people seen as having undesirable ones. It was practiced widely in the 20th century, causing enormous suffering through forced sterilizations and contributing to genocides, most horrifically the Nazi Holocaust. It is scientifically flawed because human genetics is far too complex for such crude manipulation, and because "undesirable" traits were almost always defined by prejudice rather than biology. It is ethically condemned because it treats human beings as objects to be optimized, strips people of their bodily autonomy, and invariably empowers the strong to oppress the vulnerable. Today, it stands as one of history's clearest examples of what happens when bad science meets unchecked state power.
